sites.why: Black basalt desert. Basalt is the rock of the lunar maria, such as the Apollo 11 site, and of large parts of Mars. The field also holds 14 surveyed lava caves, including the 923.5 m long Al-Fahda Cave (surveyed in 2005). Lava tubes are proposed natural shelters for future bases on the Moon and Mars.

sites.name: McMurdo Dry Valleys

sources.label: New Zealand Antarctic Soils Explorer, soil site 415 (Wright Valley, Bull Pass)
sources.quote: Soil parent material: Granite, sandstone and dolerite sandy gravel till with accessions of a few other dyke rocks
sources.note: Soil site 415 (-77.4933, 161.858) is about 3 km from our point, in Bull Pass. The same page records 'granite clasts oxidised on upper surfaces and many disaggregated' at the surface and granite clasts in the profile. It describes the glacial till the ground is made of, not the bedrock below it.

geology.note: Rock type source still to be added for basalt and ice. The ice source we had (doi 10.1002/2014JF003415) is about Beacon Valley, about 50 km away, a different valley, so under the place rule it does not count here (removed 2026-11-03, as for the ice tag in data/resources.json).

sites.why: Ice-free polar desert, among the coldest and driest places on Earth. NASA Earth Observatory says it may be the most Mars-like landscape on Earth, and NASA's astrobiology program says it has long served as an analog site for Mars.

sources.label: NASA Earth Observatory: Martian Landscape, Antarctica
NASA Astrobiology field sites

caveats: The NASA POWER surface albedo for this cell (0.56) is high for bare rock and soil, so the roughly 50 km cell probably includes glacier ice or snow around the ice-free valleys.

The 10 km terrain box around our point is mostly steep ground: median slope 14.16°, only 31.9% of the box under 10°, largest flat zone 2.0 km, relief 1,490 m (data/terrain.json). The Mars ice targets (Deuteronilus Mensae, Erebus Montes, Phoenix) are flat: median slope 0.17–0.52°, largest flat zone 9.5 km. So against them this site's terrain match is 0% and its landing match is 21% (2.0 ÷ 9.5 km). These two pillars describe the steep ground in the box, not the flat valley floors. We have not measured a point on a valley floor.
